entries.sentence: Puberty brings body and mood changes at different ages, and the NHS says a GP can advise if it seems early or late.
entries.note: Ages and GP advice from the returned NHS summaries.

entries.sentence: Puberty is the time when a child's body changes as it grows towards adulthood.
entries.note: Plain textbook definition.

entries.sentence: The pages found describe it as starting between about 8 and 13 in girls and between about 9 and 14 in boys.
entries.note: Returned summary blended several pages; puberty usually starts about 8 to 13 in girls and 9 to 14 in boys.

entries.sentence: The first signs differ between girls and boys.
entries.note: Returned summary blended several pages; signs differ by sex.

entries.sentence: Both girls and boys have a growth spurt, and both may notice changes in mood.
entries.note: Returned summary blended several pages; both sexes go through a growth spurt and may notice mood changes.

entries.sentence: In girls, the first signs are typically breast development and pubic or underarm hair.
entries.note: Returned summary blended several pages; first signs typically breast development and pubic or underarm hair.

entries.sentence: One NHS source says breast buds tend to first appear between the ages of 8 and 13.
entries.note: Returned summary blended several pages; breast buds first appear between ages 8 and 13; page attribution uncertain.

entries.sentence: Girls also have a growth spurt, and the hips become wider.
entries.note: Returned summary blended several pages; growth spurts and hip widening typical in girls.

entries.sentence: Periods usually start after these other changes have taken place.
entries.note: Returned summary blended several pages; periods usually follow breast and hair changes.

entries.sentence: In boys, the signs include a larger penis and testicles, a deeper voice and a more muscular build.
entries.note: Returned summary blended several pages; larger penis and testicles, deeper voice, more muscular appearance.

entries.sentence: Facial and underarm hair and a growth spurt are also common.
entries.note: Returned summary blended several pages; growth spurts and facial and underarm hair are common.

entries.sentence: The voice can change unevenly, and may sometimes switch between very high and very low.
entries.note: Returned summary blended several pages; voice changes can be uneven, sometimes switching high or low.

entries.sentence: One NHS teen health service also lists wet dreams, which are involuntary ejaculations, as a change that can happen in boys.
entries.note: Derbyshire teen health table listed wet dreams (involuntary ejaculations) as a change in boys.

entries.sentence: Teenagers may have mixed emotions that shift quickly, and mood swings are described as part of going through puberty.
entries.note: Returned summary blended several pages; mixed emotions that can shift quickly; mood swings.

entries.sentence: The Healthier Together guide notes that the part of the brain that helps to regulate mood is still developing.
entries.note: Search summary of Healthier Together young person puberty page.

entries.sentence: A Cambridgeshire NHS page says emotions can feel intense and that teenagers may not yet have the tools to handle them.
entries.note: Summary of the Cambridgeshire page.

entries.sentence: Early puberty can also affect how a child feels, because it can be hard emotionally to feel different from friends.
entries.note: Returned summary blended several pages; early puberty can be tough emotionally to feel different from peers.

entries.sentence: Sweat glands become more active during puberty, which can cause body odour, and extra oil in the skin can lead to greasy hair and spots.
entries.note: Returned summary blended several pages; sweat glands more active; oils lead to greasy hair and spots.

entries.sentence: Acne is common in both sexes and is linked to hormonal changes, not to dirty skin.
entries.note: Returned summary blended several pages; acne due to hormonal changes, not dirty skin.

entries.sentence: Healthier Together says periods usually start around age 12, and a later start is not usually a concern.
entries.note: Summary: periods usually start around 12, with a delay not usually a concern.

entries.sentence: An NHS page says periods often arrive about two years after breast growth begins.
entries.note: Summary: periods often about two years after breast growth begins.

entries.sentence: The first periods are often irregular, and cycles can take 2 to 3 years to settle, according to another Healthier Together page.
entries.note: Summary: first periods often irregular, cycles can take 2 to 3 years.

entries.sentence: Most girls have regular periods by 16 to 18, one of the pages says.
entries.note: Summary: most girls have regular periods by 16 to 18.

entries.sentence: The NHS page on starting your periods covers what to expect, and this site has a separate guide to periods.
entries.note: Page title returned: Starting your periods - NHS.

entries.sentence: The sources define early puberty as signs appearing before age 8 in girls or before age 9 in boys.
entries.note: Returned summary blended several pages; early puberty before 8 in girls, 9 in boys.

entries.sentence: They advise booking an appointment with a GP practice if early signs are noticed.
entries.note: Returned summary blended several pages; book an appointment with your GP practice.

entries.sentence: Some children develop certain signs early but not others, for example periods before the age of eight with no breast development, and a GP appointment is advised then too.
entries.note: Returned summary blended several pages; girls may start periods before eight with no breast development; see GP.

entries.sentence: Early puberty can sometimes cause a child to stop growing sooner than expected.
entries.note: Returned summary blended several pages; early puberty can cause stopping growing sooner.

entries.sentence: Delayed puberty is described as no breast development by around 13 or no periods by 16 in girls, and no start by around 14 in boys.
entries.note: Returned summary blended several pages; thresholds vary a little between sources: breasts not by 13 or periods not by 16 in girls; not by 14 in boys.

entries.sentence: Another NHS source advises seeing a GP if periods have not started by 15, or by 13 if there are no other signs of puberty.
entries.note: Summary: NHS guidance says see a GP if periods have not started by 15, or 13 with no other signs; page attribution uncertain.

entries.sentence: Delayed puberty is often hereditary, so a child whose parent started late is more likely to start late too.
entries.note: Returned summary blended several pages; often hereditary; parent started late.

entries.sentence: Sources also list puberty that has started but does not progress or stops abruptly, signs appearing in an unusual order, and slow growth as reasons to ask a GP.
entries.note: Returned summary blended several pages; started but does not progress or stops abruptly; unusual order; slow growth.

entries.sentence: The NHS notes that most cases are normal variation, so a GP visit is often mainly for reassurance.
entries.note: Returned summary blended several pages; most cases are normal variation; GP visit mainly for reassurance.

entries.sentence: Medicine is usually only recommended for early puberty if it is thought likely to cause emotional or physical problems.
entries.note: Returned summary blended several pages; treatment usually only if early puberty will cause emotional or physical problems.

entries.sentence: A GP may refer a child to a specialist if an underlying cause needs to be looked into.
entries.note: Returned summary blended several pages; GP may refer to a specialist.

entries.sentence: This is a routine GP appointment, not an emergency.
entries.note: Route to care statement; the NHS advice is to make an appointment.

entries.sentence: Healthier Together says Childline is free, confidential and open at any time for under-19s across the UK, and its topic pages cover puberty.
entries.note: Summary of Healthier Together Advice & Support page.

entries.sentence: Childline is free on 0800 1111, and the number does not show on a phone bill.
entries.note: Returned summary blended several pages; Childline free on 0800 1111 for under-19s; number not on phone bill; exact page uncertain.

entries.sentence: Some areas also have confidential text services for young people run by school nursing or health teams, such as one in Derbyshire.
entries.note: Summary: Derbyshire public health nurse confidential text line for young people.

entries.sentence: A GP is the usual starting point when something is worrying but is not an emergency.
entries.note: Returned summary blended several pages; GP is the usual starting point for non-urgent worries.

entries.sentence: For a mental health crisis, the NHS says to call 999 if someone's life is at immediate risk.
entries.note: Returned summary blended several pages; call 999 if life at immediate risk.

entries.sentence: For urgent help that is not life threatening, NHS 111 has a mental health option answered by trained mental health professionals.
entries.note: Returned summary blended several pages; call 111 and choose the mental health option; trained mental health professional answers.

entries.sentence: Samaritans offers free support on 116 123 at any time.
entries.note: Returned summary blended several pages; Samaritans 116 123 free 24-hour helpline.
